# The Underwater Forests: Kelp and the Coasts It Builds

## An Unlikely Forest

Most forests grow on land, but one of the most productive ecosystems on Earth grows underwater. Kelp forests are dense stands of brown algae that rise from rocky seafloors toward the surface. They sway in the surge of the sea. Divers who enter one describe a cathedral. Shafts of green-gold light fall between long stalks, and a canopy ripples overhead. Fish hang in the water like birds in a tree, and the whole structure moves slowly with the swell.

The word "forest" is more than a metaphor. Like a terrestrial forest, a kelp forest is built by a few large organisms that shape the physical conditions around them. They provide shelter, food, and three-dimensional structure to hundreds of other species. Remove the dominant organism and the community changes completely. This essay looks at what kelp is, where it grows, who lives in it, and why it has become both a symbol of coastal ecological health and a cause for concern.

## What Kelp Is, and What It Is Not

Kelp is not a plant, though it looks like one. It belongs to the brown algae, a lineage that diverged from the ancestors of land plants well over a billion years ago. Brown algae evolved large, complex bodies independently of plants. The group's brown or olive color comes from a pigment called fucoxanthin, which masks the green of chlorophyll and helps the algae capture the blue-green light that penetrates seawater.

The name "kelp" usually refers to large brown seaweeds in the order Laminariales. There are about thirty genera and a hundred or so species. They share a basic body plan with three parts. The holdfast is a branching, root-like mass that grips rock. The stipe is a flexible stalk resembling a stem. The blades are leaf-like fronds that do most of the photosynthesis. The holdfast is a common source of confusion. It does not absorb nutrients the way roots do. It only anchors the alga. Kelp takes nutrients directly from the water through its whole surface.

Giant kelp, *Macrocystis pyrifera*, is the largest of them. It can reach thirty to forty-five meters in length, and individual fronds can grow roughly half a meter in a day under good conditions. Few organisms of any kind grow that fast. To hold the fronds up toward the light, giant kelp has small gas-filled bladders called pneumatocysts at the base of each blade. Each one works as a little float. Together they lift the canopy into a floating mat at the surface where sunlight is strongest.

Bull kelp, *Nereocystis luetkeana*, takes a different approach. A single long stipe ends in one large float, shaped like a bulb, with a cluster of blades streaming from it like hair. Bull kelp is an annual. It grows from a microscopic stage in spring, reaches full length by late summer, and is torn away by autumn and winter storms. Other kelps, such as the sea palm and the many species that make up the understory, are shorter and often perennial.

## A Strange and Efficient Life Cycle

Kelp reproduces in a way that surprises people who think of it as a simple seaweed. The large, visible kelp is called the sporophyte, and it is only half of the life cycle. Mature sporophytes develop patches of specialized tissue that release enormous numbers of microscopic swimming spores. The spores settle on rock and grow into tiny filamentous organisms called gametophytes. These are male or female and are often just a few cells across. The female gametophytes produce eggs and the male gametophytes release sperm. After fertilization, the fertilized egg grows into a new sporophyte that begins the climb toward the light.

This alternation of generations has real ecological consequences. The microscopic gametophytes can survive for long periods in poor conditions, sometimes waiting through warm water or heavy shading until things improve. Scientists often describe them as a seed bank of sorts. When nutrients rise, temperatures drop, and light reaches the bottom, the gametophytes can quickly produce a new generation of kelp. That helps explain why a forest can recover remarkably fast after a storm, and why it sometimes fails to recover at all when conditions stay wrong for too long.

## Where Kelp Grows

Kelp has strict requirements, and those requirements decide where forests can exist. It needs hard substrate to hold on to, which means rock rather than sand or mud. It needs light, so it grows only in relatively shallow water, usually less than about thirty meters deep, and less in turbid water. And it needs cool, nutrient-rich water. Most kelps do poorly when water temperatures stay above about twenty degrees Celsius for long periods, partly because warm surface water tends to be depleted of nitrogen.

These conditions are met along temperate and polar coasts on both sides of the planet. The great kelp forests lie along the Pacific coast of North America from Alaska to Baja California. They also grow off Chile and Peru, South Africa and Namibia, southern Australia and Tasmania, New Zealand, parts of Japan and Korea, and the North Atlantic coasts of Europe and Canada. Many of these regions share one feature: cold, deep water rises to the surface, a process called upwelling. Upwelling brings in nitrate and phosphate and keeps the water cool enough for the kelp to thrive.

Because the forests depend on this circulation, they are sensitive to changes in it. In years when upwelling weakens, as in strong El Niño events, kelp can decline sharply across entire regions. The big El Niños of 1982 to 1983 and 1997 to 1998 stripped kelp from large areas of the California coast. In most cases the forests came back, but each event showed how tied the ecosystem is to ocean physics.

## A Crowded Community

Part of what makes a kelp forest valuable is its vertical layering. Ecologists often describe it in strata. The canopy is the floating mat at the surface. Below it is the midwater region of stipes. Beneath that, the understory has smaller kelps and other algae near the bottom. At the base are the encrusting layers on the rock, where sponges, tunicates, and coralline algae cover the surfaces.

Each layer supports its own residents. In the canopy, small crustaceans graze on the fronds, and the surface mat shelters juvenile fish. Seabirds rest in the canopy and hunt in it. Among the stipes live schooling fish, including rockfish and the bright orange garibaldi of California. Kelp bass, sheephead, and surfperch patrol the middle waters. Along the bottom, abalone, sea stars, crabs, and lobsters forage. Sea slugs, which people often call nudibranchs, crawl across the algae and rock in colors that seem too vivid to be natural.

Many species depend on kelp for part of their lives, particularly as juveniles. Young rockfish, for example, shelter in the canopy and midwater, where the dense fronds hide them from predators. The forest is a nursery for animals that spend their adult lives elsewhere. Fisheries that seem unconnected to kelp can therefore rely on it indirectly. Estimates of the economic value of kelp forests, from fisheries support, tourism, and other services, run to billions of dollars per year, though these numbers carry large uncertainties.

Kelp also feeds the system in a less visible way. Fronds wear down constantly, losing fragments that drift away as detritus. Storms tear off whole plants and send them drifting to open water or onto beaches. This material feeds communities far from the forest. Sandy beaches that look barren often depend on wrack, the heaps of kelp washed up on shore, to support the sand hoppers, flies, and shorebirds that live there. In deeper water, sinking kelp feeds animals in canyons and on the seafloor, carrying energy from the sunlit zone to places that have almost none of their own.

## The Otter, the Urchin, and the Trophic Cascade

The best-known story in kelp ecology is about a predator that most people find charming. Sea otters live along the North Pacific coast. They have the densest fur of any mammal, up to a million hairs per square inch, because they have no blubber and depend on trapped air in their coats for warmth. That same fur made them valuable. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, fur hunters killed otters across their range. By the early twentieth century, a few small remnant populations were all that remained, and the animal was close to extinction.

Without otters, the coastal ecosystem shifted. Sea urchins, which otters eat, multiplied. Urchins graze on kelp, and when their numbers grow unchecked they can strip a forest down to bare rock. The result is called an urchin barren: a seafloor covered in spiny animals, with little else alive. Barrens can persist for decades, because the urchins can survive on very little food by shrinking their bodies and waiting.

In the 1970s, the ecologist James Estes and his colleagues compared islands in the Aleutian Islands of Alaska. Islands where sea otters remained had dense kelp forests and small, scarce urchins. Islands without otters had urchin barrens and almost no kelp. The comparison suggested a causal chain: otters eat urchins, fewer urchins means more kelp, and more kelp supports more fish and other species. This kind of chain, in which a predator at the top shapes the abundance of organisms several steps below it, is called a trophic cascade. The kelp forest became one of the standard examples in ecology textbooks.

The picture has grown more complicated since then. Researchers have found that in some places other predators, such as sheephead fish, spiny lobsters, and sea stars, also keep urchins in check, and that kelp forests can persist without otters when those predators are healthy. Disease, storms, and temperature all affect how the pieces interact. Still, the central lesson holds. A single species can have effects out of proportion to its numbers, and losing it can transform a whole ecosystem.

## When Forests Disappear

In the last decade, kelp forests in several parts of the world have declined dramatically, and the causes show how many pressures can combine.

The clearest example comes from the northern California coast. Around 2013, a wasting disease swept through sea stars along the Pacific coast, killing billions of them. One of the hardest hit was the sunflower star, a large and voracious predator of urchins. Almost at the same time, an unusual mass of warm water, nicknamed "the Blob," settled over the northeastern Pacific and lasted for several years. The warm water carried fewer nutrients, which stressed the bull kelp. With the sunflower stars gone, purple urchins increased enormously. Within a few years, an estimated ninety percent or more of the bull kelp along parts of the northern California coast had vanished, replaced by urchin barrens. The loss hurt the red abalone fishery, which had been a major recreational activity, and it hurt local economies that depended on it.

Similar declines have occurred elsewhere. Off eastern Tasmania, giant kelp forests have shrunk by well over ninety percent in recent decades. This coincided with warming from the intensifying East Australian Current, along with the arrival of a long-spined urchin that has moved south as waters warmed. Parts of Western Australia, Norway, and Japan have seen their own declines, some linked to warming and some to overgrazing or poor water quality. Not every kelp region has declined. Some forests have stayed stable or even expanded, which reminds us that local conditions matter. But the pattern of losses in the most studied regions has alarmed many scientists.

What makes these losses hard to reverse is that urchin barrens can be a stable alternative state. Once the kelp is gone and the urchins are abundant and hungry, the system tends to hold. Even if the water cools and nutrients return, the urchins keep young kelp from getting a start. Ecologists call such a persistent shift a regime change, and breaking it often takes active intervention.

## Kelp and People

Humans have long relied on kelp. Archaeologists have suggested a "kelp highway" hypothesis: that early people might have moved along the Pacific coast from Asia into the Americas more than fifteen thousand years ago, following a continuous band of productive kelp forest that offered food at each step. The idea is debated, and the evidence is hard to preserve because ancient coastlines are now underwater. Still, many coastal peoples, from the Haida to the Chileans, have long used kelp for food, tools, and fishing gear. Hollow bull kelp stipes, for example, have been used as containers and fishing lines.

Today the main commercial uses are industrial. Kelp contains alginate, a gelling substance that thickens and stabilizes many products. It appears in ice cream, salad dressing, toothpaste, paints, textiles, and medical dressings, usually without any mention on the front of the package. Kelp is also eaten directly, especially in East Asia, where species such as kombu and wakame are staples. Kelp farming has grown rapidly, much of it in Asia, and has begun to expand in North America and Europe. Farmed kelp needs no fresh water, fertilizer, or land, and it absorbs nutrients from the surrounding water. Proponents see it as a promising food and feed source, and as a possible tool for local water quality.

Kelp has also drawn attention as a climate tool. The reasoning is that kelp absorbs carbon dioxide as it grows, and some of that carbon sinks into the deep sea or sediment, where it could stay locked away for centuries. This is sometimes called "blue carbon." The picture is far from settled. Measuring how much kelp carbon actually reaches long-term storage is difficult, and estimates vary widely. Most scientists agree that kelp forests are valuable for many reasons, but caution against treating them as a ready solution to carbon emissions. Protecting an existing forest is clearly worthwhile. Whether farming or planting kelp at scale would meaningfully offset emissions remains an open question.

Forests also protect coasts. A dense kelp canopy dampens waves, reducing the energy that reaches shore and slowing erosion. This effect is modest compared with that of a reef or a seawall, but it adds to the list of services the forests provide.

## Restoration

Because lost forests can stay lost, restoration has become an active field. The most direct approach is to remove urchins. Divers cull them by hand, often with hammers, in a way that is slow and labor-intensive but effective in small areas. In parts of California, Tasmania, and elsewhere, divers have cleared patches of barren and watched kelp return within months. Some programs pay commercial divers to harvest urchins or create markets for them. Urchins in barrens are often starved and have little of the roe that makes the species edible, so some projects hold them in tanks and feed them to fatten them up before sale.

Other approaches include planting kelp on lines or on seeded substrates, and a method called "green gravel," in which small rocks are seeded with kelp spores in a lab and then dropped onto the seafloor. Reintroducing predators, such as sea otters or sea stars bred in captivity, is another option. Sea otters have recovered in parts of California, Oregon, and Washington, and areas with otters have often held onto kelp better than neighboring areas without them.

None of these methods can work at the scale of the losses, which spread across hundreds of kilometers. Culling by divers may keep a few hectares healthy at a time. For that reason, scientists emphasize that restoration works best alongside protection of the conditions kelp needs: clean water, healthy predator populations, and a stable climate. Ultimately, a planet that keeps warming will make cold-water forests harder to maintain wherever they are.

## Reasons for Hope

The story is not only one of loss. Kelp is resilient, grows fast, and responds quickly when conditions improve. Some forests have rebounded after long absences. Marine protected areas have helped in some regions by preserving predators and reducing fishing pressure. Heat-tolerant kelp strains exist in nature, and researchers are studying whether populations from warmer sites could be used to reseed declining forests. Public interest has grown, too. Citizen science groups, divers, fishers, and Indigenous communities have taken part in monitoring and restoration, bringing attention and labor that science alone could not supply.

## Conclusion

A kelp forest is easy to overlook because it lies out of sight, beneath the surface of cold water, in places few people visit. Yet it is one of the most productive and structurally complex ecosystems on the planet. A fast-growing alga, a handful of predators, and a few thousand square kilometers of rock and cold water together make something that nurses fish, feeds beaches, shelters otters, and supports coastal economies.

The history of kelp forests is also a lesson in how fragile such systems can be. They depend on balances among predators, grazers, temperature, and nutrients, and when one piece is disturbed the others can shift in ways that are hard to reverse. At the same time, the speed with which kelp can recover gives some reason to think the damage is not always permanent. The future of these forests will depend on whether people can protect the conditions that let them grow, and whether they can act early enough to keep the forests from tipping into barrens that last for decades.
